conversation.content:
Hi there—thank you for coming in. I’m Dr. Morales, a perinatal mental-health clinician, and I’m glad we’re meeting today. I know the first weeks and months with a new baby can feel like a roller-coaster of emotions and questions, so my role is simply to listen and help you sort out how you’re doing.

To do that, I’ll be using a short, well-studied questionnaire called the **Edinburgh Postnatal Depression Scale**—you might hear it called the EPDS for short. It’s just ten questions that ask how you’ve been feeling in the past seven days. It isn’t a test and there are no right or wrong answers; it simply helps us spot things like low mood, anxiety, or signs you might benefit from extra support. Everything you share stays confidential between you and our care team, unless you tell me something indicating immediate risk to yourself or your baby, in which case we would talk together about next steps to keep you safe.

We can take this at whatever pace feels comfortable. I’ll read each question aloud conversationally, and you can tell me the response that best fits. Ready to begin?

Here’s the first one:

Over the past seven days, have you still been able to look forward to things, or did you find yourself not really enjoying the activities you used to?

Honestly... most things feel pretty flat. I used to get excited about little stuff—like meeting a friend for coffee or even just watching a show I liked—but lately it's like, "What's the point?" I still go through the motions, and once in a while I'll smile at something the baby does, but that happy spark I used to feel just isn't really there.
I have been able to laugh and see the funny side of things

Yeah… I mean, I can still laugh sometimes, but it feels forced or kind of distant. Like, my partner made a joke last night and I chuckled, but it didn’t feel natural—more like I was doing it because I “should.” I haven’t had one of those real belly laughs in weeks.
I have looked forward with enjoyment to things

Not really… I can tell myself, “It would be nice to get out for a walk,” but when the time comes it just feels like another chore. Even planning to meet my sister for lunch—something that used to excite me—now feels more like something I “should” want rather than something I actually look forward to.
I have blamed myself unnecessarily when things went wrong

Yeah… I catch myself doing that a lot. Like, if the baby’s fussy and I can’t settle him right away, my head jumps to “I’m failing as a mom.” Or I’ll spill a little pumped milk and suddenly I’m the worst mother ever. I know logically it’s not rational, but the guilt still hits hard.
I have been anxious or worried for no good reason

Pretty much every day. I’ll be sitting there, baby’s asleep, nothing’s wrong, but my heart’s racing and I’m running through all the ways something bad could happen—what if he stops breathing, what if I drop him, what if I’m doing everything wrong. There’s no real trigger, the thoughts just show up and I can’t shut them off for a while.
I have felt scared or panicky for no very good reason

Yeah… a couple of times this week I’ve suddenly felt like I can’t breathe, like this wave of panic just crashes over me. Once I was folding laundry and the baby was napping—everything was quiet—but my chest got tight and I had to sit down because I thought I might pass out. It passed after a few minutes, but it left me shaky the rest of the evening.
Things have been getting on top of me

Most days, honestly. It feels like the second I finish one thing—feeding, changing, trying to sleep—there’s another pile of stuff waiting. I’ll look around the living room and just feel this heavy pressure, like I’ll never catch up. Sometimes I have to sit on the couch and stare at the wall because if I try to tackle it all at once I feel like I’m going to break down.
I have been so unhappy that I have had difficulty sleeping

Yeah… I lie down exhausted, but my brain won’t shut off. I keep replaying everything I think I messed up that day, or imagining emergencies with the baby. It takes me forever to fall asleep, and then I jerk awake at every little sound, heart pounding, sure something’s wrong. Even when my partner takes a night shift, I still wake up anxious.
I have felt sad or miserable

That pretty much sums up most of my days. I’ll just be sitting there feeding the baby and feel this heaviness settle in. Sometimes it’s a dull ache, sometimes it’s sharp enough that I have to blink back tears. I keep thinking, “I should be happy—he’s healthy, I’m lucky,” but the sadness just sits on my chest anyway.
I have been so unhappy that I have been crying

Yeah… it’s happened a couple of times this week. Yesterday I put him down after a feeding and he spit up all over the clean onesie I’d just wrestled on him, and I just started sobbing. It wasn’t about the spit-up—it was like that tiny thing cracked open everything I’d been holding in. I cried until my throat hurt, then felt guilty for wasting time when I could’ve been sleeping.
The thought of harming myself has occurred to me

…A few times, yeah. It’s not like I have a plan or really want to, but when I’m up at three a.m. and everything feels hopeless, the thought sort of flashes—like, “What if I just weren’t here?” It scares me enough that I push it away, but it’s popped into my head maybe once or twice this week.

It sounds as though the past weeks have felt heavy and gray, with joy replaced by a constant sense of dread and inadequacy. You described forcing smiles, feeling overwhelmed by everyday tasks, lying awake tortured by worries, and sobbing over small mishaps while still caring devotedly for your baby. Your honesty about the scary flashes of not wanting to be here shows how exhausted and desperate you feel right now; please know these thoughts are common when depression and anxiety take hold postpartum, and help is available to ease this burden.
**Screening Impression:** Total EPDS Score: 25, Risk Level: Probable depression, urgent referral (concerns include <sym>Patient reports only forced, distant laughter and no genuine enjoyment for weeks, aligning with "Definitely not so much now"</sym>, <sym>Patient expresses near-complete loss of anticipatory pleasure, describing once-enjoyable plans as burdensome chores.</sym>, <sym>Patient describes frequent, intense self-blame for minor infant-care issues, matching "most of the time"</sym>, <sym>Patient describes near-daily, intrusive, uncontrollable worries without triggers, matching 'Yes, very often</sym>, <sym>Patient describes sudden panic attacks with physical symptoms (breathlessness, chest tightness) occurring multiple times without triggers, matching "Yes, sometimes"</sym>, <sym>Patient describes feeling overwhelmed "most days," unable to keep up with daily tasks, and needing to shut down to avoid breaking down—matching the highest level of inability to cope.</sym>, <sym>Patient describes nightly insomnia with racing anxious thoughts and frequent awakenings, matching "Yes, most of the time"</sym>, <sym>Patient describes persistent sadness throughout most days, emotional pain, and tearfulness—clearly matching "Yes, most of the time."</sym>, <sym>Patient describes multiple crying episodes this week triggered by minor stressors, indicating "quite often" level of distress.</sym>)
**Reasoning:** A score of 25 far exceeds the 14-point threshold indicating probable major depression on the EPDS. You endorsed core symptoms meeting <med>DSM-5 criteria for Major Depressive Disorder with Peripartum Onset</med>: depressed mood most days, markedly diminished interest or pleasure, guilt, fatigue, concentration difficulties, and recurrent thoughts of death. Frequent <sym>panic-like episodes</sym> and persistent <sym>anxiety</sym> suggest comorbid anxiety. Although you report no active plan or intent, the presence of <sym>passive suicidal ideation</sym> requires immediate safety planning. Contributing factors likely include sleep deprivation, hormonal shifts, and self-critical cognitions. This is a screening tool, not a diagnosis. Consult a doctor for medical advice.
**Recommended Next Steps/Support Options:**
1. Arrange urgent same-day appointment with your <med>obstetrician</med> or <med>primary care provider</med> to discuss starting treatment
2. Request referral to a <med>perinatal mental health specialist</med> for therapy and medication evaluation safe for breastfeeding
3. Create a 24-hour support plan: share your thoughts with a trusted adult who can stay with you and help with baby care while you rest
4. Call 988 (Suicide & Crisis Lifeline) or go to the nearest ED if self-harm thoughts intensify or you feel unsafe at any moment
5. Begin gentle scheduling: one small pleasurable activity or rest period each day, even five minutes, to rebuild positive experiences
6. Practice brief calming techniques (4-7-8 breathing, grounding by naming five things you see) when <sym>panic</sym> rises; consider a free mindfulness app endorsed by your provider
7. Arrange frequent check-ins-daily phone calls or texts-with your provider over the next week to monitor mood and safety
Disclaimer: This is a screening tool, not a diagnosis. Consult a doctor for medical advice.

stats.query:
postpartum depression screening impression for patient with EPDS score 25: Screening Summary – Postpartum Mood

**Symptoms endorsed:** persistent low mood, anhedonia, excessive guilt/self-blame, daily unprovoked anxiety and panic attacks, ruminative worry, frequent crying spells, sleep-onset and maintenance difficulties, feeling overwhelmed, passive suicidal ideation (no plan/intent).

**Pattern:** Symptoms present most days for at least the past week; clearly exceed “baby blues” intensity and duration; interfere with functioning and attachment.

**Screening significance:** meets threshold for probable Major Depressive Episode with peripartum onset and comorbid anxiety symptoms; passive SI elevates safety risk.

**Risk factors:** primiparous status, self-critical cognitive style, limited subjective support, sleep deprivation, prior absence of psychiatric history unknown.

**Safety:** Patient acknowledges fleeting thoughts of not wanting to be alive; denies active suicidal plan, intent, or means. Immediate safety plan and follow-up within 24–48 hrs recommended.
